episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Repair Culture & Practical Tech
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Repair Culture & Practical Tech.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who gets to leave, and who has to stay?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Advance voting days in 2026 municipal election a hit in Quesnel and Can a Former BC Liberal Unseat Quesnel’s Controversial Mayor?, plus 13 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Does self-built, self-maintained technology give a Cariboo household a real reason to stay, or is it a costly way to stay connected to somebody else's city? Topics include: Sonar accuracy, beam footprint and calibration against known depths, Power-loss protection for Raspberry Pi and home servers, including UPS and SSD options, Parcel-weighing and load-cell recalibration over time, Home server costs versus subscriptions, backup and restore procedures, Community skill retention, documentation and whether a second person can reproduce results.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cedar Crest Society for Community Living

discussion.central_question: Does self-built, self-maintained technology give a Cariboo household a real reason to stay, or is it a costly way to stay connected to somebody else's city?
discussion.riley_position: Self-reliant gear, when its skills and documentation stay in the community, gives households a practical reason to stay; the failures are fixable problems of documentation and staffing rather than proof the approach is a trap.
riley_key_evidence: The Ping2 sonar has a 100 metre range, 25 degree beam and 115 kHz transducer, with a housing rated to 300 metres in the technical guide and ArduPilot documentation.
The Geekworm supercapacitor board gives roughly 10 to 45 seconds of backup power for a clean shutdown, and an INA219 current monitor logs voltage, current and power over I2C.
A UNIHIKER K10 with a time-of-flight sensor and HX711 load cell lets a rural seller price parcels at home, saving trips into town.
discussion.casey_position: Self-reliant gear only gives a real reason to stay when the skill, record and upkeep remain local; otherwise parts, subscriptions and know-how keep the household tied to another city, and the upkeep that decides longevity is rarely documented.
casey_key_evidence: At 100 metres a 25 degree beam covers roughly a 40 metre footprint, so depth readings are averages over a patch rather than points, and the 0.5 per cent resolution figure was not confirmed.
Forum consensus holds that there is no reliable software-only fix for root filesystem corruption from hard power cuts on an SD card, pointing toward a UPS or SSD instead.
Shop-class students often leave for school after training, and the write-up gives no population figure for remote workers, so the claim that people drive for connection remains unverified.
discussion.resolution: They agreed the answer depends on whether the skill and method stay in the community: Riley argued the leave case is fixable, and Casey agreed the record is valuable but insisted on the test of whether someone who didn't build the gear can reproduce the calibration, leaving the question open pending a one-lake trial.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the BlueRobotics Ping2 sonar actually support the "up to 100 meters" depth claim in the lakebed-mapping article?

Findings: The 100 m figure is confirmed, but it is a measurement range, not a depth rating. BlueRobotics and several retailers list a 100 m range with a 25° beam and a 115 kHz transducer. The technical guide and ArduPilot documentation list a 300 m depth rating for the housing, so the sonar's limit is the acoustic range, not the housing. I could not verify the "0.5% resolution" figure from the article in the sources I checked, so treat it as unconfirmed. The article's "Clay Builds" and "Cy Antony Ash" names also differ, and I did not resolve which is the correct maker attribution.

Suggested angle: Riley can point to this as proof that a budget boat built from a 3D-printed hull and a commercial $100-range sonar can produce real bathymetric data, with the Ping's Arduino-friendly interface doing the heavy lifting. Casey can push on the distinction between "measures 100 m" and "maps a lakebed to 100 m": a 25° beam at depth covers a wide footprint, so accuracy depends on GPS fixes, boat pitch and roll, and calibration against known depths. Good material for asking what a hobbyist survey is actually good for compared with a professional echosounder survey.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does a supercapacitor UPS HAT really protect a Raspberry Pi 5 SD card from sudden power loss, and what do experienced users recommend?

Findings: The Geekworm UPS Scap 5V5A is designed for ride-through of seconds to a few minutes, not hours. Coverage describes it as built to save data and shut down safely, not to keep the Pi running. A separate guide estimates a 10 to 45 second shutdown window for supercapacitor boards, depending on capacitance and attached peripherals such as USB drives and cameras. Raspberry Pi Forums threads repeatedly say there is no reliable software-only fix for root-filesystem corruption from hard power cuts. The forum consensus is a UPS plus proper shutdown software (NUT is named), or moving the root filesystem off the SD card onto a USB drive or SSD. One Reddit user reports no corruption in their own tests, which is a useful anecdotal counterpoint.

Suggested angle: Riley can argue that a roughly $-level add-on board with a power-loss GPIO signal and an INA219 power monitor turns a fragile Pi into something deployable in a shop, kiosk, or field station. Casey can argue that the board only buys seconds, so the real fix is architectural: move storage off the SD card. That makes the debate concrete: is the repair a clever hardware patch, or a sign that a consumer SD card was the wrong foundation? Note the forum advice that a UPS only helps if outages are short, which tests how far "practical tech" can go before it needs a different design.

ELECTION RESEARCH: 2026 B.C. provincial general election

Background for the roundup's election stories and any race the hosts mention. It is not the deep dive's subject.

**Cariboo-Chilcotin**

Candidates on the filed list, per the roll-call sources: Kathryn Askew (BC NDP), Lorne Doerkson (Conservative), Douglas Gook (BC Green). The Elections BC candidate report lists all three for this riding (elections.bc.ca candidate report, Oct. 2026). Studio X News carries the same three (studioxnews.ca, final candidate list).

- **Kathryn Askew (BC NDP).** 100 Mile Free Press (Oct. 1, 2026) reports she is a retired school teacher from Canim Lake, named the NDP candidate in a party news release. It says she has 32 years in education, served in leadership roles with the BC Teachers' Federation and her local union, and volunteers with local fire, legion and community clubs. The same article says she has received a national teaching award. No previous election run by Askew has been established in the sources checked.
- **Lorne Doerkson (Conservative).** Sourced background: MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin since 2020, first elected as a B.C. Liberal, re-elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). Vancouver Sun reports he was first elected in 2020 with 51.25 per cent of the vote, running for the B.C. Liberals (Vancouver Sun, undated in snippet). Elections BC's 2020 statement of votes shows him at 6,600 votes (51.25%) (elections.bc.ca statement of votes, 2020). The Ashcroft-Cache Creek Journal (Oct. 20, 2024) reports he crossed the floor on May 31, 2024 to join the B.C. Conservatives and was re-elected in 2024. BC Ballot gives the 2024 Conservative margin in the riding as 7,722 votes (bcballot.ca). The Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026) reports he took over as Conservative leader and is leading the party into this election. No controversy involving Doerkson was established in the sources checked.
- **Douglas Gook (BC Green).** My Cariboo Now (Oct. 6, 2020) reports this was his fourth run for the BC Greens in the North Cariboo riding. The Elections BC 2020 statement of votes shows him at 707 votes, 6.38%, in Cariboo North (elections.bc.ca statement of votes, 2020). Caledonia Courier (Oct. 2024) reports he had run unsuccessfully four times in North Cariboo, including a 2017 Nechako Lakes bid where he took about nine per cent. CKPG Today (Sept. 13, 2024) announced him as the Green candidate for Nechako Lakes in 2024. He is also described as a Quesnel resident. No controversy was established in the sources checked.

**Prince George-North Cariboo (includes Quesnel)**

Candidates on the filed list: Sheldon Clare (Conservative), Denice Bardua (BC NDP), Randy Thompson (BC Green). The Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports the list was confirmed by Elections BC after nominations closed on Oct. 3. CKPG Today (Oct. 3, 2026) lists the same three.

- **Sheldon Clare (Conservative, incumbent).** Sourced background: won the riding for the B.C. Conservatives in 2024 (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports he won 11,430 votes, or 56.82%, in 2024, ahead of independent Coralee Oakes at 21.84%. Times Colonist (Jan. 8, 2026, Canadian Press) reports he said he was running for the B.C. Conservative leadership, and CFJC Today (Feb. 28, 2026) reports he and fellow MLA Steve Kooner withdrew from that race. Prince George Citizen (June 29, 2026) reports he was named the party's house leader. No controversy involving Clare was established in the sources checked.
- **Denice Bardua (BC NDP).** CKPG Today (Sept. 24, 2024) reports she was announced as the NDP candidate for this riding in 2024. Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports she finished third in 2024 with 17.03%. BC Ballot lists her in the riding (bcballot.ca). Business in Vancouver's 2024 riding brief describes her as an employee of the Quesnel school board. No controversy was established in the sources checked.
- **Randy Thompson (BC Green).** Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports he finished fourth in 2024 with just over four per cent of the vote. BC Greens' candidate page (bcgreens.ca) says he ran as the Green candidate in this riding in 2024 and previously served two years on the party's provincial council. PG Daily News (Oct. 11, 2026) reports the Greens announced him as the candidate. No controversy was established in the sources checked.

**Roster and articles**

The My Cariboo Now article on First Nations leaders and a candidate over alleged residential school denialism (Oct. 13, 2026) does not name a candidate for either of these two ridings in the excerpt I could read. The version I read names a candidate in a different riding, so I have not attached it to either race. The My Cariboo Now B.C. NDP climate pledge article (Oct. 13, 2026) names no candidates in the excerpt.

The show has not yet established any previous election run for Kathryn Askew.
